title: High-Alert Medications & Safe Administration: Anticoagulation (LVN Scope)
subtitle: 72 y/o female on warfarin with a supratherapeutic INR and bleeding signs — the LVN must recognize the high-alert risk, hold and report, protect against bleeding, and stay within scope
nursesNote: 0900 - 72 y/o female, on warfarin for atrial fibrillation (a high-alert anticoagulant). This morning she has new bruising on her arms, her gums bled while brushing her teeth, and her urine looks pink (blood-tinged). She mentions she took over-the-counter ibuprofen (an NSAID) last night for a headache. Her INR this morning is above the therapeutic range. Vital signs are currently stable and she is alert and oriented. The LVN practices under the direction of the RN/provider.

steps.title: Recognize Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) findings that BEST indicate a problem with the client's anticoagulation.

opts.text: The INR is above the therapeutic range (supratherapeutic)
opts.rat: An INR above the therapeutic range means the blood is too 'thin' (over-anticoagulated), raising the bleeding risk.

opts.text: New bruising, bleeding gums, and pink (blood-tinged) urine
opts.rat: Bruising, gum bleeding, and hematuria are signs of bleeding — the major adverse effect of anticoagulants.

opts.text: The client took over-the-counter ibuprofen (an NSAID) for a headache
opts.rat: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk and interact with warfarin — an important, correctable contributor.

opts.text: Vital signs are currently stable
opts.rat: Stable vitals are reassuring but do not address the anticoagulation problem revealed by the INR and bleeding.

opts.text: The client's pain is controlled
opts.rat: Controlled pain is unrelated to the anticoagulation concern.

opts.text: Skin over the sacrum is intact
opts.rat: Intact skin is a reassuring, unrelated finding.

opts.text: The client is alert and oriented
opts.rat: Intact orientation is reassuring, not a sign of the anticoagulation problem (though a change would be concerning).

steps.title: Analyze Cues
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) statements that correctly reflect the reasoning and the LVN's role.

opts.text: Warfarin is a high-alert anticoagulant; an INR above the therapeutic range means too much anticoagulation and an increased bleeding risk, and the bruising, bleeding gums, and hematuria are signs of that adverse effect
opts.rat: High-alert medications carry a heightened risk of serious harm; the INR and bleeding signs together indicate over-anticoagulation.

opts.text: The next warfarin dose should be held and the provider notified; the LVN does not adjust the warfarin dose independently — the provider adjusts it based on the INR, and vitamin K is the reversal agent if ordered
opts.rat: Holding and reporting is correct; dose adjustment and ordering reversal (vitamin K) are provider decisions.

opts.text: Bleeding precautions (soft toothbrush, electric razor, fall prevention) and avoiding NSAIDs and aspirin reduce bleeding risk
opts.rat: These precautions and avoiding drugs that increase bleeding protect the anticoagulated client.

opts.text: The LVN should give an extra dose of warfarin to 'catch up'
opts.rat: More warfarin would worsen the over-anticoagulation and bleeding risk.

opts.text: A high INR means the blood is clotting too much and the client needs more anticoagulant
opts.rat: The opposite: a high INR means the blood is too 'thin,' so more anticoagulant is dangerous.

opts.text: The LVN should independently adjust the warfarin dose based on the INR
opts.rat: Adjusting the warfarin dose is a provider decision, outside the LVN's scope.

steps.title: Prioritize
steps.inst: Drag these possible findings from MOST concerning (1) to LEAST (5).

opts.text: A new severe headache with confusion or one-sided weakness
opts.rat: In an over-anticoagulated client, these can signal intracranial bleeding — a life-threatening emergency and the most concerning.

opts.text: Supratherapeutic INR with active bleeding (gums and blood-tinged urine)
opts.rat: A high INR with active bleeding indicates significant over-anticoagulation needing prompt action.

opts.text: New bruising (ecchymosis) on the arms
opts.rat: A visible sign of bleeding tendency, concerning but less acute than active bleeding or neuro signs.

opts.text: The client took an NSAID last night
opts.rat: An important, correctable contributor to bleeding risk, but not an acute finding itself.

opts.text: A small cut that bled briefly and stopped with pressure
opts.rat: Minor bleeding that resolved is the least concerning of these findings.

steps.title: Generate Solutions
steps.inst: Select the THREE (3) actions that are appropriate and within the LVN's scope.

opts.text: Hold the next warfarin dose and notify the provider of the supratherapeutic INR and bleeding signs
opts.rat: Holding the high-alert medication and escalating is the correct action for over-anticoagulation with bleeding.

opts.text: Institute bleeding precautions (soft toothbrush, electric razor, fall prevention), teach the client to avoid NSAIDs and aspirin, and monitor for further bleeding
opts.rat: Bleeding precautions and teaching reduce the risk of harm while the anticoagulation is corrected.

opts.text: Apply the rights of medication administration and use an independent double-check for high-alert medications, and document and report
opts.rat: High-alert medications warrant the rights plus an independent double-check to prevent errors.

opts.text: Give the scheduled warfarin dose as usual
opts.rat: Giving warfarin with a supratherapeutic INR and active bleeding would worsen the harm.

opts.text: Independently adjust or increase the warfarin dose
opts.rat: Warfarin dose adjustment is a provider decision, outside the LVN's scope.

opts.text: Encourage the client to keep taking ibuprofen for comfort
opts.rat: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk and interact with warfarin; they should be avoided.

steps.title: Take Action
steps.inst: Drag the actions from FIRST (1) to LAST (5).

opts.text: Assess the client for bleeding (skin, gums, urine, stool) and check vital signs and level of consciousness
opts.rat: FIRST — gather data on the extent of bleeding and rule out signs of serious/internal bleeding.

opts.text: Hold the next warfarin dose
opts.rat: SECOND — do not give more anticoagulant when the INR is high and the client is bleeding.

opts.text: Notify the provider of the supratherapeutic INR and bleeding signs using SBAR
opts.rat: THIRD — escalate so the provider can adjust the dose and order reversal (vitamin K) if needed.

opts.text: Carry out ordered interventions within scope (e.g., administer ordered vitamin K, implement bleeding precautions), using read-back for verbal orders
opts.rat: FOURTH — implement ordered treatment and precautions correctly.

opts.text: Document and provide teaching (bleeding precautions, avoid NSAIDs, report bleeding), and continue monitoring
opts.rat: LAST — document, teach, and keep monitoring for further bleeding.

opts.text: After the dose was held and ordered vitamin K was given, the INR trended toward the therapeutic range and the bleeding stopped
opts.rat: A falling INR with resolved bleeding shows the intervention corrected the over-anticoagulation.

opts.text: The client verbalizes correct bleeding precautions and states she will avoid NSAIDs and aspirin
opts.rat: Correct teach-back reduces the risk of future bleeding events.

opts.text: The client develops a severe headache with new confusion and one-sided weakness
opts.rat: These can indicate intracranial bleeding in an over-anticoagulated client — a life-threatening emergency; escalate immediately.

opts.text: Staff gave the scheduled warfarin dose despite the supratherapeutic INR and bleeding
opts.rat: Administering more anticoagulant was a serious error that must be corrected and reported.

opts.text: The provider was notified, orders were carried out within scope, and bleeding is being monitored
opts.rat: Prompt escalation and correct within-scope care support a safe outcome.

opts.text: A small amount of gum bleeding persists, but there are no new bleeding sites and vital signs are stable
opts.rat: Minor persistent bleeding without new sites or instability is a holding pattern — continue monitoring.

opts.text: The INR is being rechecked per order and remains elevated but is improving
opts.rat: A downward-trending INR on treatment is the expected improving course.

opts.text: The client's blood pressure and heart rate remain stable with no signs of major bleeding
opts.rat: Stable vitals with no major bleeding indicate no acute change — continue monitoring.

reference: Aligned to the NCSBN NCLEX-PN Test Plan client-need category: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies (high-alert medications and safe medication administration) using the NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model, and supporting an under-weighted LVN blueprint area (Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies is 10-16% of the NCLEX-PN exam). Concepts reflect standard nursing practice at LVN scope: recognizing high-alert medications (e.g., anticoagulants such as warfarin) that carry a heightened risk of serious harm; interpreting a supratherapeutic INR as over-anticoagulation with increased bleeding risk; recognizing bleeding as the major adverse effect (bruising, bleeding gums, hematuria, and the red-flag signs of intracranial bleeding); holding the dose and notifying the provider (the LVN does not adjust the warfarin dose — that is a provider decision based on the INR — and vitamin K is the warfarin reversal agent, given if ordered); bleeding precautions and avoiding NSAIDs/aspirin; and using the rights of medication administration with an independent double-check for high-alert medications. Specific INR targets and warfarin/vitamin K dosing follow the provider's order and facility protocol (an INR target of about 2.0-3.0 is typical for atrial fibrillation but is confirmed against the order). Apply within current BVNPT regulations and facility policy, which can change. Lab and vital-sign values use standard reference ranges and are illustrative for the scenario; exact clinical figures are marked for faculty confirmation.
